title: Replace manual Hapsland CLI parsing with Effect CLI
body:
## Problem Statement

Hapsland CLI commands and flags are parsed by several manual argv scans and a custom lifecycle parser. This duplicates facilities already available in Effect and makes consistent validation and help harder to maintain.

## Solution

Declare the supported Hapsland command surface with Effect CLI while preserving accepted invocation, output and lifecycle behavior.

## User Stories

1. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to invoke each supported command with its existing arguments, so that I can automation continues to work.
2. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to receive generated accurate help, so that I can discover supported operations.
3. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to receive bounded errors for unknown commands or options, so that I can correct mistakes safely.
4. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to have empty and missing values rejected, so that I can avoid accidental default selection.
5. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to have conflicting host and release options rejected, so that I can avoid mutating the wrong installation.
6. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to keep machine-readable stdout stable, so that I can parse results reliably.
7. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to keep retired or unsupported hook inputs quiet, so that I can avoid disrupting agent runtimes.
8. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to run login without leaking credentials, so that I can authenticate safely.
9. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to retain both supported flag-value spellings, so that I can reuse existing scripts.
10. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to dispatch updates and repairs to the selected package, so that I can preserve installation ownership.

## Implementation Decisions

- Use Command, Flag and Argument from the installed stable Effect CLI exports; inspect pinned package APIs rather than relying on old RC examples.
- Replace overlapping argument scans and the custom lifecycle parser with one declarative command model. Do not retain a parallel legacy parser.
- Inventory accepted public and internal hook invocations before replacement; preserve accepted syntax, default host selection, host agreement and release-option exclusivity. Retired invocations retain their specified quiet behavior, not a revived compatibility path.
- Keep command handlers as existing Effect workflows, with caller ConfigProvider and scoped resources. Keep hook JSON/stdin and protocol-specific output under their existing contracts.
- Generate public help from command declarations. Preserve stdout/stderr separation, machine-readable output and exit semantics; do not print generic CLI help into hook responses.

## Testing Decisions

- Primary seam: existing real CLI subprocess contracts and lifecycle/setup subprocess journeys. Test external inputs, output, exit status and absence of side effects rather than parser internals.
- Cover every supported operation family, both flag spellings, unknown/duplicate/missing/empty/conflicting arguments, help, JSON output and quiet hook paths.
- Reuse offline credential and installation fixtures; preserve independent settings and test that invalid arguments do not mutate installations or invoke Jev.
- Run typecheck, build and the affected CLI, setup, credential and lifecycle suites; perform packed CLI smoke checks because the installed command is the user boundary.

## Out of Scope

No new commands, host profiles, release channels, consent behavior or authentication mechanisms. No redesign of JSON contracts, JSONC parsing, Bend adapters or IPC schemas.

## Further Notes

Owner-requested follow-up to the completed Effect 4 migration (#114). Stable Effect cohort is exactly 4.0.0. Jev Decision integration and Config/ConfigProvider already exist; preserve them. Native macOS validation is separately deferred to #172; this refactor does not establish new platform support. Respect the maintained architecture and TypeScript decision-boundary ledger. Preserve concurrent edits and remove superseded production implementations. Acceptance requires the stated behavior and checks, not merely importing Effect modules.

title: Replace manual Bend–TypeScript boundary validation with Effect Schema
body:
## Problem Statement

The canonical and import-graph adapters validate constructors, fields, numeric bounds and lists with hand-written decoders. Their TypeScript types are maintained separately from runtime validation, despite Effect Schema being the selected boundary tool.

## Solution

Define auditable schemas/codecs at the Bend–TypeScript adapter boundary, preserving strict validation and the existing canonical authority.

## User Stories

1. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to submit valid canonical events, so that I can retain the same Bend transitions.
2. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to receive valid commands, so that I can execute admitted work correctly.
3. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to reject malformed constructor tags, so that I can prevent invalid reducer data from escaping.
4. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to reject missing and excess fields, so that I can keep contracts exact.
5. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to reject unsafe or out-of-range integers, so that I can preserve Bend numeric limits.
6. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to reject oversized lists, so that I can bound decoder work.
7. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to preserve probability word encoding, so that I can avoid changing rule decisions.
8. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to retain immutable snapshots, so that I can prevent accidental state mutation.
9. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to reject copied foreign state, so that I can preserve resident state identity fences.
10. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to have types inferred from schemas where practical, so that I can avoid duplicated structural definitions.

## Implementation Decisions

- Define Effect Schema boundary models for canonical and import-graph event/command representations and decoded projection facts; use transformations where the Bend constructor/list representation differs from TypeScript.
- Preserve exact field policy, Nat 48-bit constraints, safe integer checks, byte-sum bounds, positive-ID requirements, probability finite-range and negative-zero handling, bounded lists and currently supported bigint conversions.
- Keep generated Bend as sole policy authority. Shape and representation validation must not become a second implementation of admission, dispatch, cache or delivery policy.
- Preserve atomic publication, state registration/provenance, snapshot immutability and existing public failure semantics. Schema decoding does not replace identity checks or physical resource fences.
- Keep pure adapters synchronous where required by atomic commits, using synchronous Schema decoding. Inspect recursive list decoding for bounded work and stack safety; do not replace a bounded iterative decoder with unbounded recursion.
- Delete superseded manual structural validators after equivalent schemas are in place; retain only necessary representation conversion and identity/native checks. Do not bump version-one formats.

## Testing Decisions

- Primary seam: existing public canonical and import-graph adapter tests and authority/conformance checks. Observe accepted/rejected values and transition/command outputs, not schema implementation details.
- Exercise malformed constructors, missing/excess fields, numeric boundaries, invalid probability words, oversized/malformed lists and supported bigint behavior.
- Preserve existing immutability, copied-state rejection and retained snapshot tests; keep generated Bend artifacts/proofs unchanged unless a separate requirement authorizes a policy change.
- Reuse deterministic canonical traces and existing performance declarations to detect material adapter overhead; never relax existing budgets to make the refactor pass. Run typecheck/build and relevant authority checks.

## Out of Scope

No change to Bend policy, generated reducers, public wire versions, cache scheduling policy or resource accounting. No CLI, IPC request migration, generic Cache replacement or unnecessary wrapping of pure functions in Effect.

## Further Notes

Owner-requested follow-up to the completed Effect 4 migration (#114). Stable Effect cohort is exactly 4.0.0. Jev Decision integration and Config/ConfigProvider already exist; preserve them. Native macOS validation is separately deferred to #172; this refactor does not establish new platform support. Respect the maintained architecture and TypeScript decision-boundary ledger. Preserve concurrent edits and remove superseded production implementations. Acceptance requires the stated behavior and checks, not merely importing Effect modules.

title: Unify resident IPC request validation with Effect Schema
body:
## Problem Statement

Resident IPC responses already use Effect Schema, but requests use a large set of manual guards and JSON checks. Maintaining the two styles increases the chance of drift at a security-sensitive runtime boundary.

## Solution

Decode all supported resident IPC requests through explicit Effect schemas, retaining the version-one transport contract, strict rejection and existing identity/authority fences.

## User Stories

1. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to send a valid resident request, so that I can retain current operation behavior.
2. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to reject malformed requests before execution, so that I can avoid unintended work.
3. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to reject retired ticket requests, so that I can keep the current contract singular.
4. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to reject wrong route-operation combinations, so that I can prevent ambiguous dispatch.
5. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to reject excess and missing fields, so that I can preserve exact envelopes.
6. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to respect frame and collection bounds, so that I can keep transport work bounded.
7. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to retain credential and ownership checks, so that I can prevent unauthorized handoff.
8. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to preserve exact host response envelopes, so that I can keep runtime integrations reliable.
9. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to retain disconnect and cleanup behavior, so that I can avoid leaked work.
10. As a Hapsland user or contributor, I want to use the caller context across native socket callbacks, so that I can preserve Clock and ConfigProvider.

## Implementation Decisions

- Define version-one request schemas for the exact current route/operation alternatives, with inferred TypeScript types where practical. Preserve existing strict excess-property policy and defaults/optional fields for each accepted variant.
- Replace manual structural request guards with Schema decoding. Keep bounded JSON framing before decoding, preserving pre-decode transport limits and malformed-input behavior.
- Encode structural field bounds, formats and cross-field validity in schemas or explicit schema refinements. Keep dynamic lifetime, identity, authorization, credential generation and canonical decisions in their current owners.
- Retain response schemas and wire shape. Preserve accepted Claude block envelopes, waiter ownership and composed turn-end finish restrictions; do not reintroduce retired ticket paths.
- Preserve listener-captured Effect Context, scoped sockets, caller Clock/ConfigProvider, disconnect cancellation and physical shutdown fences. No change to protocol version or framing.

## Testing Decisions

- Primary seam: existing resident protocol conformance tests; reuse real local socket/client-server tests to verify accepted requests, rejection responses and absence of handler execution for invalid input.
- Cover every accepted operation variant, wrong route-operation combinations, retired requests, unknown/excess/missing fields, invalid bounds and malformed/oversized frames.
- Preserve existing child identity, bounded background waiter, finish-decision and exact Claude host-envelope tests. Test externally observable behavior rather than schema implementation.
- Reuse IPC Context and disconnect/shutdown fixtures; run typecheck/build, protocol, client/server, socket framing and affected resident conformance tests. Keep tests deterministic, offline and source/credential safe.

## Out of Scope

No new wire operations, protocol version, RPC framework, ticket compatibility, authority rules or changes to transport timing/resource budgets. No CLI or Bend adapter migration.

## Further Notes

Owner-requested follow-up to the completed Effect 4 migration (#114). Stable Effect cohort is exactly 4.0.0. Jev Decision integration and Config/ConfigProvider already exist; preserve them. Native macOS validation is separately deferred to #172; this refactor does not establish new platform support. Respect the maintained architecture and TypeScript decision-boundary ledger. Preserve concurrent edits and remove superseded production implementations. Acceptance requires the stated behavior and checks, not merely importing Effect modules.

title: Build a shared Bend Monkey Business engine with first-class deterministic faults and expanded resident scenarios
body:
## Current status — 2026-10-04

Incomplete shared-simulator epic; decomposition already exists as #178–#200. #178 is the entry task that can start now. The child task specifications may be implementation-ready while their prerequisites remain open; only dependency-free slices should carry `ready-for-agent`. Existing generated orchestration and reviewed baseline cases are inputs to the migration, not proof that the shared Bend engine is complete. #203 is a downstream optional-game laboratory. This epic does not establish installed-runtime or release support.

## Task scope and prior planning

**Purpose:** Specify the shared Bend Monkey Business simulator, expanded business scenarios, deterministic fault injection, dashboard integration, and optional game consumer.
**Status:** Decomposed into #178–#200; shared-engine implementation remains open, starting with #178. Existing baseline orchestration is not completion evidence.
**Authority:** Owner-agreed feature scope, with implementation acceptance and technical proposals distinguished below. Deferred items and the pending diagnostic-depth decision are not approved implementation scope. Existing Hapsland product contracts remain authoritative for review/advice behavior; this issue does not change those contracts or establish native support.
**Expected use:** Split this feature into coherent implementation tasks and verify each slice against the shared public simulation boundary.
**Lifecycle:** Keep this issue's scope and acceptance current through implementation. At completion, consolidate enduring API and simulation guidance into the Monkey Business and dashboard documentation, transfer authoritative product decisions to their existing owners, update links, and delete superseded temporary research/handoff artifacts.

## Problem Statement

The dashboard is the primary window into Hapsland business logic, but Monkey Business does not yet generate and exercise all important resident scenarios. Its TypeScript environment orchestrator and the native Bend game's environment driver independently interpret product commands and schedule simulated completions. They share Canonical and some task scheduling, but not one complete simulation engine.

This split leaves consequential bugs outside the currently proved transitions. A previous TypeScript simulator bug issued `Started` followed by `NeverSent`; Canonical correctly rejected that contradiction, request slots remained occupied, and switching back to healthy outcomes did not restore advice. The bug was found through simulator behavior and fixed with regression tests, not discovered by the existing Bend proofs.

The owner needs sufficiently powerful, reproducible business experiments: multiple advicees competing within one resident, supersession, reuse/cache, lifetime and delivery behavior, and deliberately failing dependencies. Faults must be first-class scenario inputs. Replay and scenario tests must let an engineer investigate safety and progress without relying on a reset. A comprehensive runtime diagnostic subsystem is a separate pending decision below.

## Solution

Make Monkey Business a shared deterministic simulator implemented in Bend, calling the actual Canonical and ImportGraph decision cores. Use it headlessly, through a thin generated-JavaScript TypeScript boundary in the dashboard, and directly from the optional native Bend game.

The shared engine owns source-free workload generation, virtual time, ordered simulated effects and callbacks, business scenario orchestration, scripted/seeded faults, observations and replay. Scenario tests check the agreed behavior; the extent of in-run diagnostic checks and their dashboard presentation remains a separate pending decision. The dashboard exposes these business concepts directly. The game translates a continuous workload into its own explanatory presentation and translates game interactions into ordinary simulated-environment inputs. Game concepts never enter the shared engine or dashboard.

Scope is one resident at a time with many opaque advicee identities. Agent sessions and subagents are mapped by edge adapters; the engine has no subagent hierarchy. Resident crash recovery and persistence are excluded: an actual process death loses in-memory state and a new resident starts fresh. Recovery tests here concern transient faults while the same resident remains alive.

## User Stories

1. As a maintainer, I want one Bend simulator used by all consumers, so that business experiments do not depend on which presentation runs them.
2. As a dashboard user, I want to configure and run a continuous workload, so that I can inspect long-running review and advice behavior.
3. As a dashboard user, I want business terms throughout the UI, so that game mechanics do not obscure product behavior.
4. As a maintainer, I want the simulator to call production Canonical, so that experiments exercise actual decision logic.
5. As a maintainer, I want simulation and policy to have separate ownership, so that synthetic effects do not create another policy implementation.
6. As a user, I want several advicees within one resident, so that I can observe shared-resource contention and isolation.
7. As an adapter author, I want to map agent sessions and subagents to opaque advicees, so that the engine stays independent of runtime attribution details.
8. As a user, I want configurable per-advicee arrival rates, sizes, task boundaries and repair responses, so that I can generate diverse workloads.
9. As a user, I want correlated and repeated review inputs, so that reuse, cache and their isolation rules are exercised.
10. As a user, I want overlapping edits and explicit supersession, so that old callbacks and findings can be checked against newer revisions.
11. As a user, I want advicee disconnect, departure and resumed activity scenarios, so that one participant's lifecycle does not damage others.
12. As a user, I want shared preparation and Jev-slot pressure, so that queues, admission and releases are visible.
13. As a user, I want modeled preparation and import graphs, so that exclusions, incompleteness and resource limits remain observable.
14. As a user, I want prospective pre-edit permits and unused/expired permits, so that admission is exercised before and after edits.
15. As a user, I want Stop, continuation, collector and output-lease scenarios, so that delivery authority is exercised through the full supported simulation path.
16. As a user, I want notice cooldown, collection, expiry and cleanup scenarios, so that non-finding outcomes are represented correctly.
17. As a user, I want cache hit/miss, admission, eviction and invalidation scenarios, so that successful reuse does not conceal accounting or freshness errors.
18. As a user, I want shared-evaluation member and waiter lifecycle scenarios, so that leaving one member does not incorrectly cancel another's work.
19. As a user, I want quiet-round, inactivity and lifetime-fence scenarios, so that stale work cannot re-enter current ownership.
20. As a user, I want to inject failures while a run is active, so that I can explore a developing incident without resetting it.
21. As a user, I want to target a particular advicee, operation, request or output attempt, so that a failure affects exactly the intended work.
22. As a user, I want deterministic random fault campaigns, so that interacting failures can be explored beyond hand-authored examples.
23. As a user, I want scripted faults at exact boundaries, so that a known interleaving can be reproduced.
24. As a user, I want delayed, reordered, suppressed and duplicate callbacks, so that lifecycle fences are challenged.
25. As a user, I want callbacks arriving after cancellation, so that requesting cancellation is not mistaken for guaranteed callback disappearance.
26. As a user, I want never-sent, backend failure, timeout and interruption outcomes, so that each request lifecycle is exercised.
27. As a user, I want credential unavailability, restoration and rotation, so that temporary failure differs from changed authority.
28. As a user, I want source/input freshness changes at preparation, settlement and final handoff, so that stale delivery is tested at its real boundaries.
29. As a user, I want failed, uncertain and expired output attempts, so that reoffer and acknowledgment behavior can be inspected.
30. As a user, I want explicit fault removal and recovery phases on existing state, so that a reset cannot hide a stuck resident.
31. As a user, I want healthy advicees to progress while other advicees remain faulty, so that isolation is checked under failure.
32. As a user, I want to pause, step and run to a bounded virtual endpoint, so that I can inspect the transition that matters.
33. As a user, I want live controls applied at precise step boundaries, so that UI timing does not make experiments irreproducible.
34. As a user, I want already issued results, deadlines and committed batches preserved unless explicitly targeted, so that profile changes do not rewrite history.
35. As a user, I want workload, fault and outcome randomness separated from rendering, so that presentation does not change an experiment.
36. As a user, I want a replay containing initial configuration, identities and ordered actions, so that headless and dashboard runs reproduce each other.
37. As an engineer, I want exported replay and scenario test results sufficient to reproduce a defect, so that I can investigate it without a new diagnostic artifact or dedicated replay UI being required.
38. As a maintainer, I want independently derived test expectations, so that rerunning Canonical is not the correctness oracle for Canonical.
39. As a maintainer, I want scenario tests to detect forbidden intermediate behavior, so that a later successful drain does not hide a defect. A comprehensive runtime checker is not required until its diagnostic scope is agreed.
40. As a maintainer, I want bounded recovery checked under stated healthy conditions, so that lack of progress is distinguished from unavailable prerequisites.
41. As a maintainer, I want native Bend and emitted JavaScript compared at the same public boundary, so that both execution lanes have consistent behavior.
42. As a maintainer, I want relevant general laws and false mutants checked, so that simulation guarantees extend beyond selected examples.
43. As a user, I want the simulator to expose limit settings that already exist in production, so that experiments reflect supported product configuration. New limit configurability and simulator-storage budgets are deferred TODOs, not requirements of this feature.
44. As a game consumer, I want the continuous Monkey Business workload instead of authored waves, so that the game consumes the shared engine.
45. As a game author, I want geometry, towers, buildings, combat and economy wholly game-owned, so that I can reshape the game without changing business architecture.
46. As a maintainer, I want the application and dashboard to build and work with the game absent, so that the game is genuinely optional.
47. As a maintainer, I want superseded simulation paths and the separate scheduler package removed after transfer, so that the final state has one simulation owner.
48. As an engineer, I want coverage, assumptions, simulated faults and native evidence distinguished, so that a passing run does not claim unsupported guarantees.

## Implementation Decisions

### Ownership and execution boundary

- Monkey Business is the shared simulation owner. Organize its Bend implementation into small workload, queue/time, environment/effects and observation modules; do not grow Session into one monolithic file. Use independent test expectations without mandating a new standalone runtime-checker architecture.
- Preserve useful Session scheduling logic as an internal workload module. Move its consumers to the shared owner and remove the obsolete separate scheduler package once replaced.
- Canonical remains the product decision authority; ImportGraph remains its supporting traversal decision model. Simulated environment code supplies trusted facts, executes simulated commands and reports outcomes. This feature does not reassign reviewed native product decisions or migrate real production IO into Bend.
- Use actual production decision functions, not copied policy. Maintain an explicit coverage map separating shared production functions, modeled host orchestration and native boundaries not exercised. Newly covered resident behavior is simulation coverage, not proof that every production TypeScript callback path matches it.
- Preserve the useful public operations for create, step, bounded advance, controls, observation subscription and replay. The dashboard TypeScript boundary handles value validation/encoding, browser interaction and display; simulation scheduling/state transitions live in Bend. Native consumers import the same Bend source.
- One resident has multiple opaque advicees and correctly attributed lifetime, round, operation, request, evaluation and output identities. Agent-runtime and subagent attribution belong to edge adapters. Do not add a core subagent tree or multiple-resident model.
- Keep simulator state, generated source-free facts and replay independent of physical filesystem, sockets, credentials and live Jev. Facts supplied by the simulated environment are trusted inputs; native attribution/authenticity is not the goal of this feature.
- No new runtime dependency is required for TigerBeetle. BORROW its deterministic simulation testing architecture; REJECT its database, consensus/quorum model and VOPR runtime as Hapsland dependencies.

### Workload and scenario coverage

- Support ongoing seeded per-advicee tasks, edits, finish attempts, bursts, suspension and repair responses. Workload and size controls apply at recorded boundaries. Independent random streams cover workload variation, outcome sampling, preparation facts and fault selection.
- Expose production-configurable limits in their corresponding scenario slices: edit permit limits per advicee/resident and import graph limits. Apply existing production validation and capture rules. Production execution slots are presently fixed at eight preparation jobs and eight Jev requests; global/per-partition logical capacity is also fixed by production defaults. Preserve these facts in the standard production profile. Existing test/scenario overrides may remain explicitly labeled synthetic, but this feature does not add new production settings or claim those limits are production-configurable.
- Game waves are removed. Finite scripts and bounded test endpoints remain available in the generic scenario API; they are not wave mechanics.
- Provide generated orchestration and directed scenarios for every family below. A manually injected raw Canonical fixture alone is insufficient to mark generated-environment coverage complete.

| Family | Required generated/direct scenario coverage | Observable acceptance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Admission and concurrency | Several advicees; pre-edit permits with existing configurable per-advicee/resident limits; successful/failed/duplicate edits; unused/expired permits; shared preparation/review slots and fixed production capacity defaults | Correct round creation/joining, bounded admission, exact releases and no cross-advicee attribution |
| Preparation/imports | Multiple units; exclusions; missing/unsupported targets; configured file/tree/read/work/depth/deadline limits; incomplete evidence; callbacks during supersession | Actual decision-core commands and omissions, correct accounting and explicit outcomes |
| Revision/freshness | Same and changed inputs, members of a generation, overlapping preparation/review, newer edits before old completion, final handoff freshness change | Stale results remain accounted for as required but do not become unauthorized current advice |
| Reuse/cache | Join/claim/release; cache hit/miss; cache pressure/eviction; applicable input/configuration/credential/partition distinctions; one or all members departing | Production identity scope is preserved, shared work is settled correctly, payload ownership and logical reservations agree |
| Collection/authority | Eligibility, ordering, suppression, collectors, background-writer claims/waiters and expiry; modeled IPC response-authority lifetime and round fences | Only eligible current authorized selections reach output; no stale collector or expired writer acquires authority |
| Stop/output | Pending work wait/cutoff, cancellation, byte/token limits, continuation budget, provisional release, successful/failed/uncertain output, lease expiry, late acknowledgment and permitted reoffer | Exact committed membership, valid terminal outcomes, no duplicate certain delivery or leaked transient ownership |
| Notices/retention | Notice creation/cooldown/collection, finding and notice expiry equality, lifetime cleanup, quiet-round/inactivity transitions | Expected notices and cleanup without fabricated findings or interference with another advicee |
| Participant lifecycle | Disconnection/departure, released membership, resumed fresh activity, stale lifetime/round callbacks, remaining participants under continuing load | Isolation, proper cleanup and conditional progress of unaffected eligible work |

- Reuse and cache scopes come from current contracts. Identical inputs across participants must not silently introduce cross-partition sharing that production forbids. Both valid reuse and expected isolation/refusal are scenarios.
- Delivery profiles model the existing Edit/Background/Stop and runtime-specific authorization/continuation semantics using business facts. Raw Claude/Codex event parsing, host tool-loop emulation and native compatibility remain separate. Name profiles by behavior/runtime, not invented format versions.
- Do not invent new backpressure, retry, fairness or output policies to make scenarios pass. If an existing contract leaves required behavior unresolved, expose it as an owner decision and scoped implementation task rather than treating simulator behavior as specification.

### Live event and fault injection

- Faults are first-class typed scenario inputs. Support explicit scripts, live controls and seeded generation through one injection boundary. Each action identifies its target, trigger, kind, parameters and applicability interval; observations record whether and when it took effect.
- Target advicees, operations, requests, evaluations, collectors, writers and delivery attempts without leaking game objects into the engine. Support workload injection of fresh edits, finish attempts and participant lifecycle actions.
- Model temporary/permanent unavailability, finite delays/hangs with declared deadline behavior, failure/timeout/interruption, callback hold/release/drop/duplicate/reorder, post-cancellation completion, authority/freshness changes and failed/uncertain output. Combining faults is supported; conflicting interventions have deterministic precedence and produce an explicit application/refusal observation.
- A UI action takes effect between atomic simulation steps. Record its virtual time and global action sequence. Equal-time ordering is explicit and replayable. Seeded schedule exploration may vary ordering through recorded scheduling choices; ordinary profile changes do not arbitrarily reshuffle already queued events.
- Changing the default profile affects future operations. Already issued outcomes/due times and committed output membership remain fixed unless a supported intervention explicitly targets them. Suppressed callbacks with no deadline may legitimately violate recovery premises; report that obligation rather than silently resolving it.
- Keep enough bounded source-free issued-effect provenance to inject a valid duplicate or late callback after first completion/cancellation. Such stimuli reach the production rejection/fencing boundary; the environment must not reject them merely because its active-request map was cleared.
- Do not patch Canonical state as an injection mechanism. Product refusal or stale-event rejection can be an expected observed result. Do not conflate a modeled external fault or expected product refusal with invalid harness input or a failed test. A detailed diagnostic verdict taxonomy and obligation UI are proposals pending owner discussion; do not implement them merely from the former wording of this issue.

### Determinism, observations, replay and limits

- The engine owns virtual time and deterministic event ordering. Pausing or rendering does not advance the business model. Bounded advancement must terminate without assuming an infinite simulation terminates.
- Avoid a silent regression in numeric inputs genuinely supported by the existing public API. Resolve native/emitted representation when moving virtual time; this is a migration constraint, not a new feature promising every numeric value in every future scenario. Report an incompatible domain change explicitly.
- Expose ordered source-free frames with time/sequence, input/control/fault identity, product events/commands, before/after projections and simulated effects. Preserve the separate identity of inner preparation traversal steps. Display projections do not affect decisions. Additional runtime checker verdict fields await the diagnostic-depth decision.
- Replay is input-oriented and binds initial configuration, advicee mapping, workload settings, seed and stream algorithms, engine/Canonical/ImportGraph identity, scripted injections, live controls, ordering choices and endpoint. Reconstruct the exact observable endpoint, including controls applied without a subsequent product event.
- Keep Hapsland-owned formats at version 1 and update in place. Reject incompatible implementation identities explicitly; do not retain a parallel engine or add migration shims merely for older pre-release replays.
- Do not introduce a new configurable catalogue of simulator-storage limits in this feature. Preserve existing limits and ordinary input validation, and use finite execution budgets for an advance or automated campaign. Additional bounds for recorded inputs/controls, scheduled effects, callback provenance, retention and diagnostics remain explicit deferred TODOs; they are not hidden acceptance criteria in other slices.
- Observation retention must not affect business outcomes or replay. Infinite interactive workloads are advanced in finite budgets; automated campaigns always have seed/event/control/time limits.
- Export and reproduce the run using the existing replay concept. A separate automatically emitted failure-witness artifact and dedicated replay/witness UI are not required in this feature. Scenario test failures should still report enough ordinary information to locate and reproduce the failing input.

### Dashboard and optional game

- The dashboard is the main business interface: configure workload/advicees, select scenario/fault plans, run/pause/step, inspect business ownership/queues/outcomes, target live injections and restore conditions. Preserve usable replay export/import and reproduction through the ordinary run API. No separate replay/witness screen or new diagnostic UI is an acceptance requirement; broader safety/progress display awaits discussion.
- Keep injected cause distinguishable from product response in ordinary observations; for example, callback delayed versus old finding rejected. Any future safety/progress presentation must reflect actual scenario assumptions, but this issue does not yet prescribe a new verdict vocabulary or obligation panel.
- Dashboard and game run independent engine instances. Identical scenario/action streams reproduce identical business traces; this issue does not introduce a synchronized shared live world.
- Game geometry, towers, roads, buildings, combat, economy and visual timing are game-owned. Its adapter may turn game interactions into supported generic environment actions, recorded in replay, but the shared engine knows neither the game cause nor game object types.
- Preserve business identity if an explanatory monster represents a work item. Game-only changes such as health or gold must not mutate Canonical. Geometry can determine when the game adapter applies a modeled effect; dashboard layout never affects engine timing.
- Remove authored wave generation and connect the game to continuous workload. No game redesign, balance or old mechanic preservation is required beyond a minimal viable continuous consumer.
- Shared code, production application, dashboard, normal builds and business test gates must not import or require the game or its assets. A verification checkout with the entire game absent must still build and pass relevant application/dashboard/simulator gates. Game validation is an optional separate gate.

## Testing Decisions

### Agreed highest seam and independent oracle

- The primary seam is one public headless Monkey Business scenario API: initial configuration/seed plus ordered controls/injections produce frames, outcomes and verdicts using the actual decision cores. The owner agreed to this boundary and to the corresponding dashboard/game interaction and live injection behavior.
- Test externally observable acceptance/refusal, scheduled/completed effects, advice eligibility and delivery, cancellation, Stop results, notices, cache/reuse outcomes and final ownership. Avoid coupling tests to private helper decomposition or generated source layout beyond required ABI/authority checks.
- Use independent input/effect bookkeeping and curated expected outcomes derived from accepted contracts. Do not obtain expected behavior by running Canonical a second time or accepting its current projection as the sole oracle. A complete second policy implementation is not required.
- Scenario tests check attribution and lifetime fencing, resource conservation, authorization, stale-output suppression, exact release and valid certain-delivery/reoffer behavior, including intermediate observations where relevant. Treat authorized uncertain reoffer according to the existing contract, not as an unconditional duplicate-output prohibition. A comprehensive always-on runtime checker and dashboard diagnostic subsystem are pending scope decisions, not prerequisites silently imposed by this paragraph.

### Safety, recovery and acceptance matrix

1. Replay exactness: same implementation identities and initial/actions/fault schedule reproduce events, commands, outcomes, times and endpoint in headless and dashboard consumers. Existing replay export/import is sufficient; no separate witness format or screen is required.
2. Execution-lane agreement: native Bend and compiler-emitted JavaScript produce identical business traces/verdicts for normal, boundary and adversarial scenarios through the same public seam.
3. Step/batch/display independence: step versus bounded advance, split advancement, pause/play speed and observation retention produce the same trace when control boundaries match.
4. Concurrent isolation: multiple advicees compete in one resident; departure, stale work and failure in one advicee do not misattribute or corrupt another's work. Progress depends on explicitly available shared capacity and scheduling opportunities.
5. Scenario-family completeness: each family in the coverage table has a generated orchestration path, directed boundary fixtures and independent expected observations. Cover before/equality/after deadline and capacity boundaries, not only happy paths.
6. Fault reachability: each injected fault is demonstrably applied at its intended boundary. Valid duplicate, held and post-cancellation callbacks reach Canonical fences. Profile updates preserve already issued facts except explicit interventions.
7. Historical regression: `NeverSent` generation supplies no start; interruption supplies valid start/interruption facts. Repeated fault-to-finding cycles regain request admission, retained findings, collection readiness and recorded output without reset or swallowed rejections.
8. Recovery campaigns: first explore faults while checking safety, then continue the same state under declared healthy dependencies. Test both suspension-and-drain of finite obligations and fresh healthy work with continuing arrivals; do not use event-queue emptiness as the success oracle.
9. Progress verdict: a scenario declares eligible obligations, fair scheduling, finite responsive delays/deadlines, current inputs, valid credentials, capacity and an available delivery opportunity. Check progress within its explicit finite test budget. Expired/stale/canceled work has a legitimate terminal outcome, not mandatory delivery. Failed prerequisites and insufficient budgets are explicit, not passes. No global 2,000 ms product deadline is introduced.
10. Partial healing: restore selected healthy advicees/dependencies while others remain faulty. Verify their progress when the accepted capacity/scheduling premises hold; no resident reset, hidden state purge or forced expiry solely to make the test pass.
11. Test sensitivity: relevant independently expected scenario outcomes or assertions detect deliberately planted accounting, stale-delivery, never-sent lifecycle and progress bugs. Reproduce them with ordinary replay/test fixtures. Do not require a new independent runtime-checker architecture or automatic witness artifact. Detecting a mutant only in a shared helper is distinguished from a law-specific failure.
12. Existing limit configuration: production-configurable edit-permit and import-graph settings retain their accepted bounds and behavior. Fixed execution/capacity values remain fixed in the production profile. No new catalogue of configurable simulator-storage limits is required; finite advance/campaign budgets prevent an unbounded invocation.
13. Consumer independence: remove the game in a disposable validation checkout and build/test the application, dashboard and simulator. Separately exercise the native game as a continuous consumer with an injected environment action.

### Laws and proof obligations

- Formulate readable law candidates for concrete implementation slices and falsify them. The owner explicitly authorizes preparing especially useful candidate laws, implementation and checked proofs before review, so review can inspect a concrete example. This is a session-specific authorization to prepare proposals, not acceptance of their statements or proof scope. Present exact quantifiers, assumptions, the bug excluded and mutation evidence; owner review determines which laws become accepted requirements. Do not weaken any existing accepted law.
- Candidate law topics, not a mandatory exhaustive theorem inventory, include deterministic queue selection, compositional advancement, suspension preserving finite effects, valid lifecycle generation/consumption, committed-fact preservation and conditional progress of a finite responsive driver. Prepare the clearest useful candidates with the relevant implementation task and take them to owner review. Do not create a separate proof programme or treat this illustrative list as pre-approved universal statements.
- State exactly which arbitrary inputs a theorem quantifies over and which premises it assumes. Do not substitute fixed examples for universal claims, or claim arbitrary infinite-schedule liveness. Complex full-environment recovery combines general proved primitives with executable scenario checks and explicit unproved host obligations.
- For candidate laws prepared for review, check the original proof and provide meaningful false-mutant/literal evidence where applicable; distinguish a shared-helper failure from the law under review. Accepted laws retain their appropriate proof gates. Keep bounded checker invocations and use the kernel verdict for general proof checks. Differential native/JS checks remain necessary because proof acceptance does not prove compiler/ABI correctness.
- Prior art includes current Monkey Business recovery/environment/replay/session conformance tests; Canonical independent traces and resident boundary tests; ImportGraph budget/progress proofs; the existing conditional request/handoff proofs and mutation runner; and TigerBeetle's separation of safety, recovery and independent state checking.
- Ordinary gates remain offline and bounded, with no live Jev or agent sessions. Record source-free evidence and limits. Simulation acceptance is not an installed-runtime/platform or complete-resident execution claim.

## Out of Scope

- Multiple simultaneous residents, distributed consensus, replication/quorum behavior or use of TigerBeetle/VOPR as a runtime dependency.
- Persistence, reconstruction of pre-crash resident state, resumption of lost answers or recovery guarantees after resident process death. A new resident starts with fresh in-memory state.
- Real filesystem parsing/capture, HTTP, IPC/socket execution, native agent tool loops, actual credentials, paid Jev and native attribution/authenticity checks. Simulated boundary outcomes and response/lifetime facts are included; native enforcement remains separately validated.
- Moving real production IO into Bend in this feature or making simulation an alternative production policy engine.
- Core subagent hierarchy, game ontology in business modules/dashboard, shared live game-dashboard networking, wave compatibility, balance overhaul or preservation of old prototype mechanics.
- New product backpressure/retry/fairness semantics without their existing contract owner's decision; missing policy must not be invented in the simulator.
- A complete independent semantic reference implementation, separate automatic failure-witness format/UI, a newly prescribed diagnostic verdict/obligation system, automatic failure minimization, exhaustive search of all schedules, formal correctness of the compiler, unbounded campaigns or guarantees that an agent/model receives or follows acknowledged advice. Broader runtime safety/liveness diagnostics remain pending discussion rather than implicitly included.
- Automatic deletion of earlier game prototypes before the owner has selected any useful mechanics. Their temporary index remains the removal guide; authored waves in the current game's consumer are removed as part of this feature.

## Further Notes

### Implementation decomposition

This is one feature specification, suitable for an epic with dependent tasks; the stages below are not separate permanent architectures.

1. Reuse and narrow the public scenario/injection/observation/replay boundary and independent test expectations. Capture existing traces and resolve numeric representation during migration. Do not make a new diagnostic taxonomy or full resource-budget catalogue a foundation task.
2. Move workload, deterministic queue/time/randomness and replayable actions into the shared Bend owner. Preserve the useful Session logic and thin public TypeScript API; delete replaced production simulation code as each slice lands.
3. Move preparation, Jev and output/finish simulated effects in small complete behavior slices. Each slice includes its dashboard/API path, replay, native/JS checks, applicable independent regression assertions and removal of replaced code. Establish historical repeated recovery and callback injection early; no late big-bang integration is required.
4. Add generated concurrent-advicee, supersession, reuse/cache, notices, collectors/waiters and lifetime/quiet cleanup scenario families. For each, reuse production decisions and record assumptions/native gaps.
5. Integrate dashboard workload/fault controls and live targeted injection with each behavior slice through the common seam. Preserve ordinary trace inspection and replay. Dashboard remains entirely business-oriented; separate witness/replay UI is not required.
6. Adapt the optional game to continuous workload and generic environment actions; remove current authored wave generation and redundant host simulation paths. Consolidate/delete the separate scheduler package and obsolete wrappers.
7. Confirm the already integrated scenario/tests and accepted proof gates, native/JS conformance, finite seeded campaigns, game-absent builds and current documentation. Final acceptance is not where replay, dashboard or conformance first starts working. Record remaining scope decisions and empirical limitations.

### Owner clarification, deferred TODOs and pending diagnostics

The 2026-10-02 review of this specification and its draft tickets found that some details had been promoted from advisory suggestions to mandatory scope without separate discussion. The owner clarified:

- Configurable limit controls are included only where production already exposes them. Preserve TODOs for new configurability of currently fixed execution/logical-capacity limits and for extra simulator-storage budgets; defer that work to separately scoped tasks. Existing production settings belong inside their admission/preparation scenario tasks, not a standalone resource-limits epic.
- Replay export and reproduction remain included. A separate diagnostic artifact or special-purpose replay/witness UI is not required now.
- Useful law implementations/proofs may be prepared before owner review, as concrete proposals. The illustrative theorem topics are not an accepted exhaustive proof contract.
- Explain safety as forbidden behavior not occurring, including during injected failures, and liveness as eligible work progressing after its prerequisites become healthy while the same resident continues. Scenario regressions for those behaviors remain included. The extent of continuously running independent checks and dashboard diagnostic presentation needs further owner discussion; do not implement the previously expanded checker/obligation taxonomy by assumption.

### Authority, prior work and provenance

- The accepted [advice/handoff contract](https://github.com/dearlordylord/hapsland/blob/master/docs/advicing-target-contract.md), including conditional progress and closure, remains the behavioral owner. Consult current configuration/review contracts and the reviewed TypeScript decision boundary when implementing each family. Synthetic runtime profiles preserve existing user-controlled delivery authority.
- This owner-requested feature resumes and expands the applicable simulation ideas in [#169](https://github.com/dearlordylord/hapsland/issues/169). It does not automatically adopt every advisory item: new storage budgets, automatic failure-witness artifacts and expanded runtime diagnostics are deferred or pending as stated above. Its old deferral does not authorize implementation by itself; this issue records the new scope decision. Keep #169 linked as predecessor and reconcile its disposition when implementation is decomposed; do not run a parallel duplicate simulator project.
- [#116](https://github.com/dearlordylord/hapsland/issues/116) owns production canonical authority; this issue consumes that authority rather than reopening the original aggregate migration. Existing unresolved policy issues remain separate contract dependencies where applicable.
- Astra independently recommended a shared simulation kernel with the former Session as a small internal workload component. The owner then chose broader resident scenario coverage, opaque advicees, first-class live faults, no crash recovery, a removable game and continuous workload without waves. The later limit/replay/law-review clarifications and pending diagnostic-depth decision above also govern this issue.
- TigerBeetle is advisory precedent, not a behavioral specification for Hapsland. BORROW production-core-under-virtual-effects, seeded and scripted faults, reproducible runs and state-preserving safety/recovery testing. Separate checkers and richer failure-witness artifacts remain advisory proposals requiring their own scope decision. REJECT database-specific replication/quorum and simulator runtime coupling.
- Primary evidence: [VOPR documentation](https://github.com/tigerbeetle/tigerbeetle/blob/6f8e6b58d1811bb21cd6ea4fb93cb2e9d77abd81/docs/internals/vopr.md), [liveness article](https://tigerbeetle.com/blog/2023-07-06-simulation-testing-for-liveness/), [VOPR scenario/liveness implementation](https://github.com/tigerbeetle/tigerbeetle/blob/6f8e6b58d1811bb21cd6ea4fb93cb2e9d77abd81/src/vopr.zig), [independent state checker](https://github.com/tigerbeetle/tigerbeetle/blob/6f8e6b58d1811bb21cd6ea4fb93cb2e9d77abd81/src/testing/cluster/state_checker.zig), and [failure categories](https://github.com/tigerbeetle/tigerbeetle/blob/6f8e6b58d1811bb21cd6ea4fb93cb2e9d77abd81/src/testing/cluster.zig). Documentation establishes upstream claims; inspected source establishes visible structure. No TigerBeetle execution was performed. Its liveness implementation also records convergence limitations; do not infer unconditional recovery.
- In the prior local investigation, existing top-level Bend proofs and ImportGraph/progress kernel checks passed; the progress runner checked 502 literal instances, rejected 10 selected mutants and passed the kernel verdict; 21 existing simulator recovery/environment tests passed. These are evidence for the old boundaries, not validation of this unimplemented feature. The main law file then contained 336 laws, only nine with universal binders, so the old whole simulator was not formally proved.
- The temporary earlier-game index has been added to the latest game README. It identifies retained road, auto, flow and combat sources/bundles and their transfer/removal trigger. Use it before deleting earlier games; no old game is a new runtime dependency.

title: Replace CLI and boundary validation with Effect declarations
body:
Completed #173, #174 and #175: CLI invocation and both validation boundaries now use Effect declarations, with overlapping manual parsers and structural guards removed.

- CLI: declarative commands/flags and generated help preserve both flag spellings, quiet hooks, bounded errors, JSON stdout, caller ConfigProvider, credentials and selected-package lifecycle dispatch.
- Bend boundary: synchronous exact schemas and inferred models preserve numeric/probability/bigint constraints, bounded iterative lists, original-state provenance, immutable snapshots and atomic publication. An independent inventory verifies 346 constructor schemas. Generated reducers and proofs are unchanged.
- Resident IPC: exact route/operation request schemas decode after bounded framing. Invalid requests cannot reach handlers; response envelopes, listener Context, ownership/credentials and cancellation remain covered by socket tests. Formats remain version 1.

Supporting fixes isolate installation test metadata from release platform profiles, install checksum-pinned Bend/Lean during the existing CI tool-install step, and mark a stale unpublished evidence link pending publication. A preexisting launch storm is fixed by coalescing outstanding native children until physical close; equivalent Effect leaf imports reduce pre-lock loading. Original baseline also failed the one-CPU startup test; four consecutive one-CPU runs passed after these changes without relaxing deadlines or reducing the 100 callers/eight clients. Source-only hosts retain native artifacts only after unchanged release verification; arm64 compilation and probes remain unchanged.

Validation: [final Linux x64 CI](https://github.com/dearlordylord/hapsland/actions/runs/37049998774) passed docs, typecheck, all authority/proof gates, 1388 tests (2 live tests skipped; 1390 total), and build. Linux arm64 Node 24.20.0 local full suite passed 1385 tests before the final three source-build tests; those three tests and final build also passed. Packed lifecycle, clean-package credential and seven setup journeys passed, including repeated package/setup checks after the launcher fix; zero provider calls and actual HOME activation record unchanged. Independent reviews have no unresolved blockers.

The executable adapter benchmark detects overhead: 500 canonical traces moved from approximately 42–52 ms to 68–73 ms; 500 six-event graph traces from 10–18 ms to 65–76 ms on Node 24.20.0 Linux arm64. No existing test budget was relaxed. Earlier failed CI attempts exposed the supporting fixture/startup/build issues above; final CI passes.

No live Jev or additional platform support is claimed. Native macOS validation remains #172.

Closes #173
Closes #174
Closes #175
